(CNN) -- In "Street Kings," Keanu Reeves' bad-boy cop Tom Ludlow may not play by the rules, but the film sure does. Keanu Reeves, second from left, and Forest Whitaker are shifty cops in "Street Kings." The movie is textbook Cop Noir. Directed by David Ayer, who wrote "Training Day" and directed "Harsh Times," from a script that originated with "L.A. Confidential" novelist James Ellroy, it's a story both men have told before and will doubtless return to again. Too bad that story -- the one about the constant struggle with an impure world, betrayal, disillusionment, retribution, all that jazz -- isn't told with much originality this time around. As Ludlow, a detective with a special LAPD vice squad, Reeves shoots first and asks questions much, much later. In his field the bad guys are easy to spot, and if Tom has to get his hands dirty, well, then he'll be careful to wipe away the residue before he calls it in. He works from the gut. We have Ludlow's number from the beginning: He wakes up, vomits, cleans his gun, and knocks back a couple of miniature bottles of vodka. Then he crashes a kidnappers' den and puts down four gangsters before they know what's hit them. "Don't worry," he tells the distraught little girls caged up in the back. "I'm a cop." It's probably superfluous to add that he's still nursing a grievous hangover from the wife who died in flagrante with a person unknown two or three years ago. It's also probably superfluous to mention that Internal Affairs (headed by Hugh Laurie) is beginning to sniff around Ludlow's unit. In particular, IA is talking to his ex-partner Washington (Terry Crews), a revelation that sends Ludlow reaching for his baseball bat. Before he can put Washington straight, though, his old pal is gunned down before his eyes by a couple of punks. Can Ludlow cover up his own potentially incriminating presence at the scene and still track down the cop killers? Hell, yes, even if he has to alienate everyone in the department before he's through. Reeves doesn't do much "acting" as such, but he doesn't need to: His performance is clean and spare, in synch with Ayer's clipped economy, and he has a doleful quality that goes some way to redeem a nasty and wretchedly naïve character. Alcoholism doesn't appear to have thrown off Ludlow's aim any, but it must have dulled his reasoning. A broody, intuitive detective should be able to piece together this boilerplate mystery without too much head-scratching, but Ludlow never stops to look even two steps ahead. (I guess he's not a James Ellroy fan.) But what he lacks in insight he makes up for in sheer determination, not to say blood-lust. In a neat touch, when it's time to cool off his public profile for a spell, the rogue cop is transferred to a desk in the complaints department -- surely his idea of purgatory, and, obviously, an utterly pointless occupation. Forest Whitaker boosts the energy level as Ludlow's paternalistic mentor, boss, and No. 1 fan: "You're the tip of the spear," he tells him. "Who else is going to hold back the animals?" Violent and cynical and a shade or two overdetermined, "Street Kings" ably demonstrates the pitfalls embedded in the pragmatics of "a necessary evil," or anyone who sets himself up as a law unto himself, but ultimately it can't conceive of a better alternative. After all, the rest is politics, a game that even the most hard-boiled anti-hero would never lower himself to enter. And, besides, he's seen it before. "Street Kings" is rated R and runs 107 minutes. It is probably superfluous to add that he is still nursing a grievous hangover from the wife who died in flagrante with an unknown person two or three years earlier. It is equally unnecessary to mention that Internal Affairs, headed by Hugh Laurie, has begun sniffing around Ludlow’s unit.

(CNN) — Keanu Reeves plays Tom Ludlow, a renegade police officer who disregards procedure in “Street Kings,” even though the movie itself follows the familiar conventions of its genre. Reeves, pictured second from the left alongside Forest Whitaker, portrays one of the film’s morally dubious cops.

The result is a standard example of police noir. David Ayer—screenwriter of “Training Day” and director of “Harsh Times”—directed from a screenplay originally developed by “L.A. Confidential” author James Ellroy. Both storytellers have explored this territory before and will probably do so again. Unfortunately, this version brings little freshness to its well-worn themes of corruption, betrayal, shattered ideals, revenge, and the ongoing fight against a tainted world.

Ludlow is a detective assigned to a specialized LAPD vice unit. His approach is to open fire immediately and leave the questions for far later. He has no trouble identifying criminals, and whenever the job requires him to cross ethical lines, he makes sure to remove any evidence before reporting what happened. Instinct, rather than careful thought, guides him.

The opening quickly establishes his character: Ludlow gets out of bed, throws up, cleans his weapon, and drinks two small bottles of vodka. Soon afterward, he storms a hideout used by kidnappers and kills four gang members before they have time to react. Addressing the terrified young girls imprisoned in the rear, he reassures them by saying, “Don’t worry. I’m a cop.”

Predictably, Ludlow remains deeply damaged by his wife’s death. She died two or three years earlier while having sex with an unidentified person. Just as predictably, Internal Affairs, led by Hugh Laurie’s character, has started investigating Ludlow’s squad. Investigators are especially interested in his former partner, Washington, played by Terry Crews. When Ludlow learns that Washington has been speaking with IA, he grabs a baseball bat.

Ludlow never gets the opportunity to confront him, however. Before he can do so, Washington is shot dead in front of him by two street criminals. Ludlow must then conceal the fact that he was at the murder scene—where his presence could make him look guilty—while also pursuing the men who killed the officer. He is certainly willing to try, even if doing so means turning the entire department against him.

Reeves does not deliver an especially showy performance, nor is one required. His restrained, uncluttered work matches Ayer’s brisk and economical direction. He also brings a mournful quality to Ludlow that makes the unpleasant and remarkably gullible detective somewhat easier to accept.

Although heavy drinking has apparently done nothing to damage Ludlow’s accuracy with a gun, it may have weakened his ability to think clearly. A gloomy investigator who depends on intuition should be able to solve such a formulaic case without much difficulty. Instead, Ludlow rarely considers what might happen more than a couple of moves in advance—perhaps he has never read James Ellroy.

Whatever he lacks in perception, he compensates for with relentless drive and an appetite for violence. One clever detail comes when the department decides he needs to stay out of public view for a while. The rebellious officer is reassigned to a complaints-department desk, a position that must feel like limbo to him and one that is clearly of no practical value.

Forest Whitaker adds momentum as Ludlow’s protective father figure, commanding officer, and strongest supporter. He describes Ludlow as “the tip of the spear” and asks who else could keep “the animals” under control.

Brutal, pessimistic, and somewhat too determined to make its point, “Street Kings” effectively illustrates the dangers of embracing a so-called necessary evil—or of allowing someone to operate as his own legal authority. In the end, though, the film cannot imagine a preferable solution. The remaining option is politics, and even the toughest antihero would consider that arena beneath him. Besides, this is all familiar ground to him.

“Street Kings” is rated R and has a running time of 107 minutes. Entertainment Weekly’s review was available through a separate link, as was an option to email the article to a friend.

Ludlow, once comfortable bending the law, must confront the consequences of a system in which nearly everyone has adopted the same attitude.

The film draws heavily on established cop-noir themes. Its protagonist is a damaged, disillusioned officer whose violent methods make him almost indistinguishable from the criminals he pursues. Authority figures cannot be trusted, loyalty is easily manipulated, and justice is treated as something personal rather than institutional. Betrayal and retribution drive the story, while the bleak Los Angeles setting reinforces the idea that corruption has spread throughout the city and its police force.

There is considerable experience behind the production, and the cast gives the material an appropriately hard-edged tone. counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style movie review of the 2008 crime thriller “Street Kings,” starring Keanu Reeves and Forest Whitaker.
counterfactuals.output:
### Review: “Street Kings” patrols familiar turf with grit and star power

In “Street Kings,” Keanu Reeves trades his customary cool for bruised, simmering rage, playing an Los Angeles police detective whose methods are nearly as dangerous as the criminals he pursues.

Reeves stars as Tom Ludlow, a hard-drinking LAPD officer protected by his politically skilled captain, Jack Wander, played with commanding charm by Forest Whitaker. When Ludlow’s former partner is murdered, the investigation pulls him into a maze of corruption, planted evidence and divided loyalties. As Internal Affairs closes in, Ludlow must decide whether he is uncovering a conspiracy or merely confronting the system he helped create.

Director David Ayer, working from a story credited to crime novelist James Ellroy, knows this territory well: sun-bleached Los Angeles, compromised cops and violence disguised as procedure. The film’s city is not glamorous. It is a landscape of convenience stores, cramped apartments and police back rooms where the line between law enforcement and organized crime has almost disappeared.

Reeves gives one of his more physically committed performances. Ludlow is less a detective than a blunt instrument, charging into confrontations with the confidence of a man who assumes his badge will excuse the aftermath. Reeves’ restrained delivery occasionally limits the character’s emotional depth, but it also suits Ludlow’s numbness. He is a man who has spent so long rationalizing brutality that self-reflection comes as a genuine shock.

Whitaker supplies the film’s theatrical spark. His Captain Wander can be paternal, intimidating and calculating in the same conversation. Even when the story’s direction becomes apparent, Whitaker keeps the character watchable, suggesting that corruption is not just a moral failure but a management strategy.

The supporting cast is unusually strong. Hugh Laurie brings dry skepticism to an Internal Affairs investigator, while Chris Evans plays a more conventional officer drawn reluctantly into Ludlow’s search for answers. Their presence helps ground a plot that grows increasingly tangled and, by the final act, less surprising.

“Street Kings” is at its best when it treats police corruption as a culture rather than a twist. Its most effective scenes show officers casually rewriting events, rewarding loyalty and treating civilians as pieces on a board. But the movie often retreats from those implications into standard thriller mechanics: gunfights, betrayals and revelations delivered at high volume.

The result is tough, efficient and relentlessly grim, though not especially original. Viewers familiar with Ellroy’s morally contaminated Los Angeles—or Ayer’s later police dramas—will recognize nearly every street corner. Still, Reeves’ battered intensity and Whitaker’s magnetic authority give the film enough energy to keep its familiar machinery running.

**Verdict:** “Street Kings” is a solid, hard-edged crime thriller elevated by its cast, even if its investigation leads to a destination audiences may spot long before the detectives do.

**“Street Kings” (2008): A Conventional but Muscular Cop Noir**

David Ayer’s *Street Kings* operates squarely within the familiar territory of corrupt-cop noir: a morally compromised detective, a murdered colleague, an internal-affairs investigation, and a conspiracy that extends through the police hierarchy. The film rarely surprises at the level of plot, but it delivers its genre conventions with enough hostility, momentum, and urban paranoia to remain effective.

Keanu Reeves plays Tom Ludlow, an LAPD detective who is grieving his wife, drinking heavily, and accustomed to solving problems through extralegal violence. After Ludlow is implicated in the killing of his former partner, he begins an investigation that gradually exposes the corruption surrounding him. The arc is a standard one—a compromised enforcer discovering that his loyalty has been exploited—but the film’s bleakness comes from how thoroughly Ludlow belongs to the system he is investigating. He is not an innocent cop framed by bad men; he is already one of the department’s blunt instruments.

That conception bears James Ellroy’s unmistakable influence. Ellroy, who shares screenplay credit with Kurt Wimmer and Jamie Moss, returns to his characteristic Los Angeles: a city organized by tribal loyalty, racism, political expediency, and institutional rot. The police force is less a public institution than a private kingdom whose officers exchange favors, conceal crimes, and manufacture official narratives. Yet *Street Kings* is a simplified, more action-oriented version of Ellroy. It lacks the historical density, labyrinthine plotting, and feverish language of his novels or of *L.A. Confidential*. Its conspiracy eventually becomes predictable, and its dialogue sometimes substitutes hard-boiled posturing for genuine complexity.

Ayer is well suited to this material. As in his other Los Angeles crime films, he gives police work a tense, territorial quality. The action is harsh and close-range, and the city feels fragmented into hostile zones. He is particularly effective at conveying the casual normalization of brutality: Ludlow’s violence is not initially treated as an aberration but as an unofficial method tolerated by superiors because it produces results. At the same time, Ayer’s direction can be overly emphatic. The aggressive pacing, grim lighting, and repeated confrontations insist so strongly on toughness that the film sometimes resembles a stylized police procedural more than a fully developed noir tragedy.

Reeves’ performance is central to whether that approach works. His natural reserve makes Ludlow feel emotionally sealed off, and his physical stillness suits a man who has converted grief into routine aggression. Reeves does not deliver Ellroy-style dialogue with the verbal relish that a more flamboyant actor might bring, but his flat, contained manner has its own value: Ludlow seems exhausted, numb, and dangerous rather than charismatic. Some of the more heated scenes expose the limits of Reeves’ range, particularly when the material asks for explosive emotional transitions. Even so, his opacity fits a character who has spent years refusing to examine himself.

Forest Whitaker provides the film’s more theatrical counterweight as Captain Jack Wander, Ludlow’s commanding officer and surrogate father figure. Whitaker’s expansive, insinuating performance helps clarify the film’s real subject: not simply corruption, but the seduction of belonging. Ludlow’s deepest loyalty is not to the law but to the men who have protected and validated him.

As cop noir, *Street Kings* is conventional to the point of inevitability. Its betrayals are telegraphed, its supporting characters are often functional types, and its moral reckoning remains less searching than its premise promises. Still, Ayer’s forceful direction, Ellroy’s institutional cynicism, and Reeves’ bruised, withdrawn presence give the film a grimly persuasive texture. It is not a reinvention of the corrupt-cop thriller, but it is a lean and competently brutal example of the form.

## ‘Street Kings’ Review: Keanu Reeves Patrols a Familiar Beat in a Corrupt-Cop Thriller

**Spoiler warning: Major plot details follow.**

*Street Kings* dives into the shadowy world of Los Angeles police corruption with plenty of gunfire, moral compromise and hard-boiled posturing—but few ideas that haven’t already appeared in sharper crime dramas.

Keanu Reeves stars as Tom Ludlow, an LAPD detective whose grief, alcoholism and willingness to bend the law have made him both effective and dangerously compromised. Protected by his powerful captain, Jack Wander (Forest Whitaker), Ludlow routinely plants evidence and executes suspects while convincing himself that brutal methods serve the greater good.

The plot kicks into gear when Ludlow’s former partner, Terrence Washington (Terry Crews), is murdered after speaking with Internal Affairs. Ludlow witnesses the killing and quickly becomes entangled in the investigation, joining forces with detective Paul Diskant (Chris Evans). What initially looks like a gangland execution gradually reveals a conspiracy reaching deep into Ludlow’s own unit—and ultimately to Wander, whose paternal loyalty masks a sprawling criminal operation.

Directed by David Ayer and co-written by James Ellroy, *Street Kings* has the ingredients of a ferocious police noir: compromised heroes, institutional rot and a city where badges offer protection from accountability. Reeves gives Ludlow an appropriately exhausted, emotionally sealed-off presence, while Whitaker supplies theatrical menace as a commander who treats corruption as management strategy. Hugh Laurie, playing an Internal Affairs captain, adds a dry, watchful counterpoint.

Yet the film’s central weakness is its lack of originality. The crooked-cop narrative unfolds along conspicuously familiar lines: the rogue detective, the murdered partner, the suspicious Internal Affairs officer, the trusted superior who is obviously too protective, and the late revelation that corruption extends higher than expected. Echoes of *Training Day*, *L.A. Confidential* and countless urban police thrillers are difficult to ignore, and the twists tend to confirm genre expectations rather than overturn them.

The movie also gestures toward serious questions—whether results can justify illegal policing, how institutions manufacture “good” cops, and whether Ludlow is victim or willing participant—but often resolves them through shootouts and betrayals. Ludlow’s moral awakening is compelling in theory, though the film never fully forces him to confront the damage he has personally inflicted.

As a grim, fast-moving action thriller, *Street Kings* is watchable and well cast. As an examination of police corruption, however, it mistakes cynicism for depth. Its streets may be dirty, but they have been traveled many times before.

## *Street Kings* Review: Strong Performances Patrol Familiar Ground

David Ayer’s *Street Kings* is a grim, muscular police thriller powered by committed performances from Keanu Reeves and Forest Whitaker. Yet for all its anger, violence, and moral corrosion, the film rarely escapes the conventions of the hard-boiled cop movies that came before it. Its Los Angeles is a familiar urban inferno, its hero is the familiar rule-breaking detective with a damaged soul, and its conspiracy unfolds through a predictable chain of dead partners, internal investigations, and compromised superiors.

Reeves stars as Tom Ludlow, an LAPD detective whose methods sit somewhere between aggressive policing and outright vigilantism. Introduced during a brutal operation that establishes both his effectiveness and his disregard for procedure, Ludlow is the classic hard-boiled protagonist: isolated, grieving, alcoholic, and protected by a department that values results more than legality. When his former partner, Terrence Washington, is murdered in a convenience store, Ludlow becomes entangled in an investigation that threatens to expose corruption within his own unit.

The setup is efficient, but almost every element arrives with the weight of genre precedent. Ludlow is warned away from the case, evidence is suspiciously convenient, Internal Affairs circles in the background, and the detective’s most trusted allies become potential suspects. Los Angeles is photographed as a landscape of liquor stores, dim apartments, interrogation rooms, and sun-bleached streets where institutional rot appears to have infected everyone. The film’s worldview is not merely cynical; it is nearly predetermined. In *Street Kings*, badges conceal criminals, official procedure is mostly theater, and violence is the only language that produces immediate results.

Ayer, whose screenwriting credits include *Training Day*, knows how to give this material momentum. Shootouts are abrupt and ugly rather than elegant, and the dialogue often has the clipped aggression of men accustomed to using intimidation as a professional tool. The film is at its strongest when it observes the informal codes that allow police corruption to flourish: loyalty is demanded, misconduct is reframed as necessity, and protection from consequences becomes a form of control. Ludlow’s superiors do not simply excuse his behavior; they cultivate it.

Reeves gives one of his more forceful performances as Ludlow. His characteristic emotional restraint works well for a man who has turned grief into numbness and routine. Reeves does not try to make Ludlow charming. He plays him as stiff, exhausted, and frighteningly direct, suggesting that the detective has spent so long suppressing doubt that he can barely recognize it when it returns. His physicality also suits the role: Ludlow moves through confrontations with the blunt confidence of someone who expects violence and may even find it easier than conversation.

The performance cannot entirely solve the character’s familiarity. The alcoholic cop haunted by personal loss is one of the genre’s most overused figures, and the screenplay provides Ludlow with too few qualities that distinguish him from earlier versions. His moral awakening is also somewhat convenient. The film asks the audience to accept him as both a participant in a corrupt system and the man capable of exposing it, but it does not fully explore the contradiction. Ludlow’s misconduct is often treated less as an ethical crisis than as evidence that he is a dangerous but fundamentally useful hero.

Forest Whitaker brings greater complexity to Captain Jack Wander, Ludlow’s commanding officer and protector. Whitaker alternates between paternal warmth, political calculation, and barely contained menace. Wander understands exactly how loyalty works in a compromised institution: he reassures Ludlow while reminding him that his career, reputation, and freedom depend on continued obedience. Whitaker’s performance gives the character an authority that extends beyond rank. Even when Wander is behaving supportively, there is a sense that he is managing the room and measuring everyone in it.

That ambiguity helps sustain the film, although the screenplay eventually reduces it through increasingly explicit revelations. As the conspiracy expands, *Street Kings* falls back on the familiar assumption that corruption must culminate in a single commanding villain. The institutional critique therefore becomes narrower than it initially appears. Rather than confronting a system in which routine incentives produce abuse, the film channels its outrage into one grand explanation and one final confrontation. This makes for a satisfying thriller mechanism, but a less challenging drama.

The supporting cast adds energy. Chris Evans brings humor and relative idealism to Detective Paul Diskant, who becomes Ludlow’s uneasy investigative partner. Hugh Laurie, as Internal Affairs Captain James Biggs, deploys his dry, skeptical manner effectively, though the character often functions as an exposition-delivery system and a convenient source of pressure. Cedric the Entertainer also makes an impression in a small role, lending personality to scenes that might otherwise feel purely functional.

Structurally, *Street Kings* proceeds like a checklist of hard-boiled police-thriller devices: the rogue detective, the murdered former partner, the incriminating ballistic evidence, the distrusted Internal Affairs investigator, the reluctant younger ally, the hidden network of dirty cops, and the superior officer whose concern may conceal ulterior motives. Even the film’s twists are less surprising than inevitable. Once the principal relationships are established, experienced viewers can anticipate both the direction of the conspiracy and the identity of the figure at its center.

That predictability does not make the film ineffective. Ayer maintains a tough pace, and the actors give the material more conviction than its recycled framework might seem to deserve. The violence has consequence, the atmosphere is convincingly hostile, and the central relationship between Ludlow and Wander carries genuine dramatic tension. The film also has flashes of insight into how corruption hides behind fraternity and how institutional approval can turn personal brutality into professional identity.

But *Street Kings* ultimately wants the pleasures of a dirty-cop thriller more than it wants to interrogate those pleasures. It condemns police violence while repeatedly presenting Ludlow’s violent instincts as uniquely capable of cutting through deception. It depicts corruption as pervasive, then resolves it through the exposure of a few specific offenders. And it surrounds its protagonist with moral ambiguity without fully demanding that he answer for his own choices.

The result is a solid, forcefully acted genre film rather than a revelatory one. Reeves supplies the wounded intensity, Whitaker provides the commanding theatrical presence, and Ayer delivers the necessary grime and propulsion. Yet the movie’s “street kings” occupy roads that cinema has traveled many times before.

**Rating: 3 out of 5 stars.**
